newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: FEATURE - Six months on, Kabul chafes under Taleban rule.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Six months on, Kabul chafes under Taleban rule.

text.p: In the six months since they took Kabul, the purist Islamic Taleban have ridded the city of the rampant corruption that characterised the discredited former regime and brought a degree of security.
But for the relatively cosmopolitan population of Kabul these advances have come at a high price.

On September 27, after 18 months on the southern outskirts of the city, the Taleban finally captured Kabul, hanged the last communist president, and vowed to impose their interpretation of Islamic law on the citizens of this battered and dysfunctional city.
In order to force the population to conform with their vision, the Taleban have issued a series of decrees that have impinged on every aspect of life.
WOMEN HARDEST HIT
Women have been hardest hit by the restrictions, but the Taleban's reforming zeal knows few bounds.

The Taleban have banned women from schools and all work except in the medical sector, and forced them to wear a shroud- like head-to-toe veil that leaves only a small hexagonal patch of gauze for the eyes.
The punishment for any woman who disobeys is an instant beating from the young, heavily-armed Taleban fighters who roam the streets in Japanese pick-ups.
The Taleban say that women will be allowed to go back to work and school as soon as segregated facilities can be provided, but that they lack the resources to create them.
However, they have shown little interest in taking up offers from the United Nations, among others, to help with the provision of these facilities.

The ban on women working has hit Kabul's huge population of widows and female heads of households particularly hard, a situation that has been exacerbated by the disintegration of Kabul's economy. International aid agencies have expanded their programmes to try to compensate.
Women have not been the only victims of the Taleban's Islamicisation drive.
CIVIL SERVANTS SACKED FOR TRIMMING BEARDS

Earlier this month 65 civil servants were sacked for having trimmed their beards. They had been told to grow beards that are long enough to extend below a clenched fist clasped at the bottom of the chin, and to avoid western haircuts and clothes.

There has been a slightly surreal aspect to some of the Taleban's edicts. In the last six months, they have outlawed New Year celebrations, paper bags, music, dancing, flying kites on roof tops, and have told people to paint over their windows on upper floors so that they cannot see into their neighbour's gardens.
One western observer believes that much of Taleban policy says less about Islam than about the culture of the southern Afghan villages where most of the Taleban come from.

"The Taleban seem to come up with a policy that conforms with the social norms of the areas they come from, and then invoke Islam to provide a justification after the fact." said a foreign worker in Kabul who asked not to be named.
He said the Taleban are frightened of losing control of their young, uneducated and ill-disciplined fighters.

"If they allow women to walk about without the veil or go to school, they are frightened that the idealistic village boys they are using as fighters will either become disillusioned, or take the law into their own hands." he said.
However, he says that the number of decrees hides a deeper lack of policy.
LACK OF COMPREHENSIVE POLICY

"The Taleban seem to filling a larger policy vacuum with a myriad of petty regulations which give the impression of government, but there is still no evidence they have a comprehensive plan for the future of Afghanistan." he said.

Taleban-held areas of Afghanistan are ruled by Mullah Mohammed Omar, the shadowy leader of the Taleban, assisted by a seven-man interim council and a cabinet of acting ministers. The Taleban have promised to create some sort of representative forum, but are unclear as to what form it will take.

Other countries have shown reluctance to recognise the Taleban as the legitimate government in Afghanistan. Most countries say they will wait until the United Nations makes a decision on formal recognition, something not expected until October at the earliest.

At present the Taleban control about 75 percent of Afghanistan. Six provinces in the northeast of the country are still run by an opposition alliance consisting of the ousted government, northern leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum and Shi'ite leader Karim Khalili.
The Taleban advance seems to have stalled in the face of the high passes over the Hindu Kush north of Kabul, and some recent defeats in the remote nothwestern province of Badghis.
The Taleban have been generally welcomed for bringing security and reducing corruption, and they still have solid support in the south of the country.
But there is increasing resentment in Kabul at the incursions of their draconian restrictions and the lack of material benefits from their rule.
